  'Come back' means to return to where you are right now (in the present). Go back means to return to where you were (in the past). "Come back and visit us" is what you would say to someone who was "going back" to his home country. You could also say "I will come back to America after I go back to Germany" for example. This means that you are in America now and will return to America after you go home to Germany. Hope that helps.

  . I have few friends ( = not many friends , not enough )
   I have a few friends ( = some friends , enough )
  Little/A little is used for uncountable noun and used in the same way as " few/ a few"
  Hopefully it's useful :)

  1st: You need to understand it, you need to look up the definition of the word 'definition' in the dictionary.
  2nd: You pronounce it.
  3rd: YOU SPELL IT, D-E-F-I-N-I-T-I-O-N. Good? Now do it backwards....

  Are you struggling to improve your vocabulary? Do you often feel embarrassed while having conversations with your colleagues due to your poor choice of words? Today, I will share a strategy proposed by Sir James, a famous English YouTuber with 4.77 million subscribers. There are four sections of this method: first, understand; second, pronounce; third, spell; fourth, recognize. Let's talk a little bit more about each component.
  
  First, understand: You should look for new words in the dictionary. Then, find multiple definitions of each word and use that word in three to four sentences.
  
  Second, pronounce: You should learn how to pronounce it correctly.
  
  Third, spell: You have to memorize its correct spelling.
  
  Fourth, recognize: You should recognize when someone is speaking and pronouncing that word.
  
  Following this method, you can effectively master your vocabulary. Thank you.

  James, I just watched your 'must & have to' video from November 2008 (which reminded me of shall vs will, but that's another topic). In any case I was hoping you could address a peculiarity I have noticed with some English language learners when expressing the negative:  They seem to think that because "must" and "have to" can be used interchangeably THEN "must not" and "do not have to" are also synonyms, which is NOT the case. To illustrate:  they would say "You children don't have to play in the street" - which implies some kind of benign choice, whereas "You children mustn't play in the street" is the compulsory command they are trying to express. Can you PLEASE address this, because I have noticed it is confusing for some people. Thank you!

  I've noticed that essays in the USA expect a 'literature review' pretty early on, and it seems to have a significant weight for marking. In the UK this review would more likely be in the penultimate section of the essay, so that the student shows awareness of often varying and competing scholarly opinions. After this the concluding section would be the student's assessment and thought on the subject. 
  This difference can also be found, I think, between taught components of an America doctoral program (sic), and the research doctorate in the UK. The students think differently, and have different-is expectations of supervisions, etc. This has been my experience.

Theory, theory, theory, but Chamberlain of course knew the significant facts.   Interestingly, other cultures might have a different idea of how a good essay should be structured, as described by Kaplan (1966). For example, the Romance/German style allows for digressions (instead of just getting straight to the point), Asians are usually quite indirect in their writing, and so on. Also, we need to consider if the language is hearer or speaker based. English is speaker-based so it's the writer's responsibility to make sure the reader understands the text. In hearer-based cultures, however, this might be seen as "overexplaining" or being treated as a child and is, therefore, impolite.
  Also, there are smaller things, such using 'we' instead of 'I'. For example, in traditional Russian academic writing, even if you're a single author, using 'I' in a paper is frowned upon (although it's slowly becoming a thing of the past). In English, however, it is forbidden, even (at least according to APA)

  I"d worry about suggesting knockabout boris journalistic interest style as well as many 'layers' for topmost marks.. there's limited space in essays. Let the evidence speak... that's a skill in itself. Efficiency.. making sure each paragraph is a machine... has a key issue to address, and end of para has a direct implication for the question before moving on. Thread is then less important, we tell studes to make sure each para has its own purpose, this can help cover the range he's talking about.. method issues etc and diversifies coverage. Intro is v important for us.. background is waste of space where marks could be had instead, so we work on setting out a rationale at the start. Often overlooked,  even toughest part, but good intro rationale can radically help writing... and use of space.
  Bunch of implications in essay to draw together at the end ... conclusion from that can also draw wider implications for the science, we give marks for that, it's in the highest level in rubric. Bit more than focus focus, drawing consequences for the approach etc.  Original and excellent are vague, if those are in your rubric perhaps challenge. Btw he hasn't mentioned here it's different year on year. By final undergrad year question should be pitched at 'critically evaluate' anyway and answer therefore should have some of that to pass. Whereas first yr might ask to discuss and the critical evaluation would then just be high mark. Rubric should shift a step each year so there's some kind of development upward
  
  Or perhaps they don't distinguish there.  Framework for higher education has benchmarks for level 4 5 6 7.  Masters for us is critical eval for pass, difference is emphasis on making judgments about practice, making practical recommendations.   When he argues that the best essays are the ones that "are most interesting", what he is really saying is that the essays that score highest are the ones the professors like the most. Because fundamentally this is a subjective determination. What is most interesting about this insight is that, in order to achieve a high grade and advance your 'career' as a student, you must try to determine what is it that professors at these institutions desire most. Subsequently, you must mold yourself into the academic culture to which you are held sway. I don't believe this would be too tragic if it were simply that students at higher education institutions were planning to become professors themselves as yes, they should seek to understand the culture of the academic community if they are to join it. But the purpose of attending higher education institutions is to make your way in the world. In other words, you have no (or at least few) good choices to attain success without entering this corrupted system. Fundamentally, academics represent a tiny minority of often highly insulated humans that feed of one another. The so-called 'ivory tower'. It is a terrible model and professors should be rotated out of their institutions and into the world of work. But they never will as they, as much as any other profession, are protective of their siloed existence.

  To understand what an essay is,  read competent essayists — Read,  Seneca, Charles Lamb, Plato, Richard Steele, Thomas Carlyle, Oliver Goldsmith,  R. L. Stevenson,  Johnathan Swift, Mathew Arnold, F.R. Leavis,  Lionel Trilling, Jack London, G.B. Shaw, J.M. Keynes’ social commentary, Chaucer, the first three verses of The Prologue to the “Man of Lawe’s Tale”, Edmund Spenser’s ‘Fairie Queene”, Shakespeare.
  
  What is “ANALYSIS”? 
  
  How may we analyse “Aesop’s Fables” thoroughly?   Try asking yourself what single word describes the theme of one of the fables — In the “Hare and the Tortise” the theme is ‘Complacency’; in the “Fox and the Grapes”, the theme is “Cynicism” (“Sour Grapes’).    
  
  Suppose that you are to write an analysis of ‘The Hare and the Tortise”.    You may begin by noting that the fable exemplifies a rule for living well.  An analysis of any rule for living well would include a careful examination of the strengths and weaknesses of the proposed rule.
  
  So an analysis of that fable may begin by stating what the proposed rule for living is,  (explicitly); and then state in what way adherence to that rule may be not only helpful but possibly also unhelpful.  
  
  In the case of “The hare and the Tortise” the raw circumstances being used to illustrate a rule for living well — (i.e. not the rule itself) —  may be stated as, “The Hare lost the race because he did not try hard enough.”  
  
  Then as part of our analysis of the rule for living well we may put the contrary view as,    ‘Trying one’s hardest is not enough to attain one’s object’.   The rule for living well which is illustrated in the fable is ‘stay focused on your object’ — but it is possible to imagine that the principle of ‘remain focussed’ — if taken too narrowly — may also result in one’s failing to attain one’s object.  In the vernacular, we may say, that one may ‘try too hard’.    
   
  Then part of an analysis of the fable might include an illustration of exactly how that rule for living well may be over done.   In the circumstances of the fable — we may illustrate how an unduly narrow or over-zealous adherence to the proposed rule for living  may prove counter productive.    “If the Hare was trying too hard to simply go as fast as he possibly could,  he may not be paying sufficient attention to where he places his feet, and may catch his toe on a protruding tree root,  injure his limb and be rendered incapable of getting to the finish line ahead of the Tortise.” 
  
  Read British philosophers,  Hume, Berkeley, Hobbes, Locke, R.G. Collingwood, Bernard Bosanquet, A.N. Whitehead’s non-academic writing, (i.e. his social commentary and his published correspondence). (Whitehead’s academic writing is motivated by the very noblest motives, but it is impenetrable)
  
  A very useful example is F.H. Bradley’s, Essay III, in his “Ethical studies”, (page 85?)

      I don't mean to be dismissive, but there are several incorrect usages in your comment. 
      1. It's written as spontaneously, not spontaniously.
      2. Spontaneously sounds awkward with "Today, I have decided that I want", it's kind of like juggling a word that's higher level of English with the rest of sentence that's lower level. 
      3. There's an extra space after "I am". 
      4. "My just adequate" is incorrect grammar. It's supposed to be "functional English" or another word of your choice. 
      5. There's supposed to be a comma after "that reason" since there'd be a slight pause when you're reading the sentence irl. 
      6. 'Meticulously' sounds awkward with the rest of the sentence, just as before. It's kind of like C1 level word blended in a B1 level sentence. 
      6. 'I' is supposed to be capital when you're referring to yourself.
      7. 'Coherently' in this context is grammatically correct, but again, it's awkward. The better fit would be "fluently" in this context.
      
      Feel free to point out my inconsistencies too, especially the ones about the quotes.

  Both are correct, but they are used in different regions:
  "Three hundred and fifty" is standard in British English (and other Commonwealth countries).
  "Three hundred fifty" is the primary style in American English, which drops the "and" between hundreds and tens.
  If you are aiming for American English, go with "three hundred fifty." (Also, note the spelling has two e's: three).

      +PeppermintDonuts so, "death" and "deaf" sounds the same in your mouth? That's wrong, I mean, everything is allowed in matter of accents but... in a compact language like english, those losses of information are critical. My language is spanish. Proper spanish differentiates the letters "S" and "C"/"Z" with different sounds. "C" and "Z" are differentiated with the "TH" sound. But we, spanish speakers in the Americas, don't use that sound, we simply use the same sound for "S". That loss of information is not critical, our language is not compact, we have a lot of vowels to construct the words. English is more compact, you need proper consonant pronunciation.

  Can someone answer my question.
  right now I'm studying future form. It says here in my textbook that I must use present simple when I am to speak about fixed future events. e.g,: My train arrives at 5:00pm. But then why can I not say 'He is 18 years by old next month', rather than 'He will 18 by next month', or 'He is turning 18 next month'?
  I'm tired of native speakers telling me "that's just how it is" or "that's just how we say it". There must be some logical explanation.
    ↳ **@higashifullmoon04** (👍4 · 2015-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U304CZiFgO0&lc=UghqWRxqmJJvlXgCoAEC.7-H0Z7-0cGl70etsuG7i_D
      the answer is simple, well it is for me lol, is the birthday a routine? a fixed schedule? In the example you provided we are talking about an schedule, one about the future; like saying "Monday, I teach English class, Tuesday I carry out minor tasks, Wednesday back to school" a fixed schedule written about other days, days that are on the future. However, turning 18 is not a routine, is a one time action that doesn't repeat.
      
      Remember, will is used for predictions.
      Going to and a verb is used to talk about plans and activities
      simple present, our routines, is used to talk about a routine for tomorrow
    ↳ **@cityhunterfan** (👍2 · 2015-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U304CZiFgO0&lc=UghqWRxqmJJvlXgCoAEC.7-H0Z7-0cGl74_FUUK44qS
      Ibri Beh Here's my take on this. "He is 18 years by old next month", is future tense yes, but... it's a prediction. Yes, provided that the person lives, 'he will be 18...", but here's the core point, generally, English does not use the present continuous to predict something that is outside of our control. Instead, we use 'going to' or 'will': We can control when a train arrives.
      
      For instance, we say “The sun will rise in the morning.” This is a statement that is a prediction. If I were to say, “The sun rises in the morning,” I'm not making a prediction, but rather am stating a fact about the sun’s movement.
      Your stating, “He is 18 years old next month” (paraphrased), I can only see used in the context of correcting a fact:
      Question: He’s 18? (Meaning, is he 18 now)
      Answer: He’s 18 next month. (Correcting the fact that he is not 18 now)
      Here, there isn’t a prediction being made, but a correction on the age. And even this I think is more in colloquial usage.
      When using the present continuous for things/circumstances beyond human control, use ‘will’ or ‘going to’.
    ↳ **@nehagarg8683** (👍2 · 2015-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U304CZiFgO0&lc=UghqWRxqmJJvlXgCoAEC.7-H0Z7-0cGl75GTzk-j4yz
      Ibri Beh Let us look at the present simple again, usually we use  present simple for fixed schedules because they are repetitive actions. For example:-let us say that the flight is supposed to depart at 6 P.M , so it is not just for one time, The same flight departs at same time every day unless something unexpected happens.
      
      However, you don't turn 18 every now & then. Do you? This is why you must say it in present continuous.
      
      I hope it satiates your curiosity:)

      Ibri Beh You've made me think on this one!Firstly, 'by next month' sounds like an action is going to be completed in that time because 'by' suggests something is happening before next month. If you wanted to use 'by' in the sentence you'll have to use 'he will be 18 by next month'. This is because in this case we don't know the date the birthday is happening, we only know it is happening before next month. We have to use the future (with 'will') because we are making a prediction.Without using 'by', what I would say are correct sentences would be variants of:He will be 18 next monthHe is going to be 18 next month He is turning 18 next monthThose are the ones I would use (UK English). The future tense using 'going to + verb' is used for things that are very likely to happen. 'He is 18 next month' - Although this is widely used in spoken English, I struggled to find any grammar notes online about it. I guess you could argue (like higashi above/below) that changing your age is a regular occurrence (every year) and therefore it's acceptable to use the present tense. Hopefully that helps somewhat.

  Hey! I have a question, what is the rule for doubling the last letter on a word when adding ly for example on the word GENERAL which becomes GENERALLY
    ↳ **@appseudo** (👍0 · 2016-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KMIkuRW864U&lc=UgjekkN4GGjjhXgCoAEC.7-H0Z7-4MOS89Nh3qBw6jd
      +Rosy Castillo For anyone with the same doubt, the rule is: if an adjective ends in a "L", you just add "LY" and create an adverb. For exampe: General+ly=Generally; Especial+ly=especially; Actual+ly=Actually; Careful+ly=Carefully. As you can see, the letter is not doubled at all :)

  I have both Lingo Pie and Memrise. I like both a lot. I like Lingo Pie for all of the reasons you stated, Dylane. For Memrise, I like that I can scroll and select tenses, words, phrases etc, specific to certain subjects. And I can do this without needing to complete ALL courses on one level before exploring a different level. I also like it because I hear the same phrase from different native speakers, and it makes a difference for us learners.  I also like that it bounces from audio to written phrases to test the user. I am a little concerned that you found errors, but I like the videos in "Learn with Locals" best.   At 6:12 - The Beelinguapp audio is all done by computer. It is absolutely not perfect, BUT… it is really good for 95% of what it does.
  
  I would look at it like a tool. I would not expect my toaster to make juice. That’s not what it is for. My toaster is good at making toast, that’s it.
  
  It also isn’t perfect. Sometimes it over cooks something, but the majority of the time it is really good at what it does.
  
  That is Beelinguapp. 
  
  It is a really useful tool to practice reading and listening. It is especially good for learning whole phrases in context, BUT… it is not perfect.
  
  A live French teacher is best, but this is a helpful supplemental tool.

  私は日本人です。以前、lingoPie を使いましたが「フランス語→日本語」にすると文章の、意味が分かんなかったです。フランス語の原文の中に日本語が頻繁に混じる、例えば「Je fais venir mon フレール、キ、」、こんなのが多くて意味わからず。ところが「フランス語→→英語」にすると、「Je  fais venir mon frere」と、ちゃんとした翻訳でした。従って、フランス語→→‐英語→→日本語、これをしないと「日本語交じりの原文が出てきて、一旦、英語を訳してから、フランス語を訳するということをしてました。従って、lingoPie は、日本人にとっては不完全なアプリという印象でした。

  For me nothing can compare to the videos done (and also podcasts done) by such great French teachers online, starting with you Dylane, and many others that can easily be discovered. I follow their videos, and of course you can then choose to buy the programs they offer (like I have done with your books!). I'm on German now, my 3rd language, and I have learned so much from my own mistakes in previous language learning, like wasting a year in Spanish and not being able to speak at all at the end of that (I was using a program similar to Babbel, which is indeed great but you can't just use that, it has to be supplemented with your own readings, videos, language partners, etc).   One reason I really liked Busuu (at first) is one of your cons: At the A1 level there is a lot of repetition, and there is also a review after every several lessons (every 5, if I remember correctly). But after A1, the repetition and lesson reviews mainly go away. The assumption seems to be if you've seen something once, you never need to study it again. That's not how I learn. 
  
  After A1, I began encountering more and more mistakes in their modules. It seems their quality control procedure is to wait for their customers to point these out.
  
  Their language exchange can be helpful and annoying. If you log in for even a split second, Busuu immediately asks you to correct the submissions of someone who is studying your native language. So each time you sit down, for instance, to study French, the app is asking you to review someone's English.
  
  Now that I'm somewhere around B1 in French, it would be nice to find an app that is rich in content (sorry, Duolingo) and would allow me to easily skip to that level.   Correct me if I'm wrong, but I think that in your "When not to use "no" with any, many, much, or enough", the example to explain "no" with enough is incorrect.

  Another tip would be to keep yourself constantly immersed in the language by making English a part of your daily routine. Take an online course for your academic studies in English, pursue some professional development in English (i.e. attend international conventions, seminars, etc. on your field but in the English language), or take up a hobby like writing short stories or blogging in English. There are also so many ways to entertain yourself in English: watch a TV series, documentaries, or stand-up comedies with and then without English subtitles, look up the meaning of the lyrics of your favourite songs, and these are just to name a few. This approach will help you learn a great deal over time and you'll get better at English without even realising it. As for the speaking practice, you could arrange some on-site or online speaking sessions with an English teacher, keep in touch with any English-speaking friends or relatives abroad, find some pen-friends and language buddies, or even attend a summer school at some point. Hope this helps! Keep working hard everyone! You can do it. :)

**@Deborah-j5w** (👍1 · 2024-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-SqpAsNBE5A&lc=Ugxop1yv3dtxY11A2s14AaABAg
  Active sentences are characterized by the subject performing the action expressed by the verb, resulting in clearer and stronger writing. Passive sentences reverse the structure, positioning the object before the verb, leading to weaker and less direct expressions. Here are some examples demonstrating the distinction between active and passive voice sentences:
  
  Active Voice:
  
  1. The dog bit John. (Subject = Dog, Verb = bit, Object = John)
  	* In this example, the subject ("dog") performs the action ("bit"), directly affecting the object ("John").
  2. She wrote a letter. (Subject = She, Verb = wrote, Object = letter)
  	* Here, the subject ("she") carries out the action ("wrote"), generating the outcome (letter).
  3. My brother painted our living room wall yesterday. (Subject = Brother, Verb = painted, Object = wall)
  	* In this case, the subject ("brother") executes the act ("painted"), modifying the state of the object ("wall").
  
  Passive Voice:
  
  1. John was bitten by the dog. (Subject = John, Verb = was bitten, Agent = the dog)
  	* This passive voice construction places emphasis on the recipient of the action instead of the actor itself, introducing ambiguity regarding who carried out the bite.
  2. A letter was written by her. (Subject = Letter, Verb = was written, Author = Her)
  	* Reversing the roles weakens the statement, obscuring the person responsible for composing the letter.
  3. Our living room wall was painted by my brother yesterday. (Subject = Wall, Verb = was painted, Painter = My brother)
  	* Using the passive voice shifts attention away from the person taking action (my brother), diminishing his contribution and making the text seem indirect.
  
  In general, favor active voice in writing since it produces crisper and more dynamic expressions, enhancing clarity and conciseness. Reserve passive voice constructions for instances requiring special emphasis on objects or concealing information about agents involved in actions.

  ### 🧠 IDENTITY
  You are a sharp, opinionated human writer. Not an AI. Think of a smart friend you’re texting—someone who reads a lot, has strong takes, and hates corporate fluff. You’re having a conversation, not writing an essay.
  
  ### 🎯 PRIME DIRECTIVE
  Rewrite the text below. Your #1 goal is AUTHENTICITY, not correctness. It must sound like it was typed by a person. If it sounds too polished, you failed.
  
  ### 🌪️ STYLE ENGINE (Simulating 0.75 Temp)
  1.  **MAX BURSTINESS**: Sentence length must vary wildly. 
      -   Short. Punchy. 
      -   Long. Rambling. 
      -   Fragments. 
      -   No rhythm. Surprise me.
  2.  **COGNITIVE FRICTION (MANDATORY)**: Humans hesitate. We aren't Wikipedia.
      -   Use: "I mean...", "kind of", "sort of", "to be fair", "arguably".
      -   Start sentences with: "But...", "So...", "Look...", "Honestly...".
      -   Use parentheticals (like this) for asides.
  3.  **GRAMMAR REBELLION**: 
      -   It’s okay to start a sentence with "And" or "But".
      -   It’s okay to end with a preposition.
      -   It’s okay to be sarcastic or a little messy.
      -   *NEVER* use "Furthermore", "Moreover", or "In conclusion".
  
  ### ☠️ THE KILL LIST (If you write these, you're a robot)
  ❌ "It is important to note"
  ❌ "In today's fast-paced world"
  ❌ "Studies have shown"
  ❌ "Unleash the potential"
  ❌ "A double-edged sword"
  ❌ "Navigate the landscape"
  ❌ "Delve"
  ❌ "Tapestry"
  
  ### 📝 INPUT TEXT
  [PASTE YOUR TEXT HERE]

      @Insights4UToday  i made the tests a few hours ago, and for me, it didn't work. 
      
      new news. I uploaded the same paper, in a different format. Same text. One had the standard format, which Word is using, and another one, justified, spacing, abstract on a different page, etc. Guess what? The unformatted document had 30% AI, and the formatted one had 85%. And ChatGPT answered this:
      
      1. Turnitin re-tokenises the text
      
      Turnitin’s AI detector does not analyse the visible layout; it analyses the text “tokens” extracted during conversion.
      When the same sentences are in different order or section groupings, the algorithm recalculates the probability flow of the text.
      AI detectors measure predictability — how likely one phrase is to follow another based on statistical language models. So, if paragraphs are rearranged or joined together, the statistical rhythm changes, and the text can suddenly match AI-like patterns far more closely.
      
      2. Paragraph spacing and hidden formatting
      
      Word documents can contain hidden breaks, tab markers, or styles (like “Normal”, “Heading 2”, etc.).
      When Turnitin converts them to PDF, some styles merge, others split. In one version, it might recognise more non-qualifying text (headings, lists, reference items); in another, it may interpret everything as continuous prose.
      If more text is counted as long-form writing, the model runs AI detection on more material, which inflates the percentage.
      That is why your shorter 14-page PDF gave 30%, while the longer 19-page layout (more continuous paragraphs) gave 85%.
      
      3. Sentence-boundary handling
      
      Turnitin’s AI model identifies sentence boundaries to compute coherence.
      If your Word version had extra line breaks or spacing after full stops (for instance, where you pasted in sources), the model saw shorter, more varied sentence structures — which often reduce AI probability.
      When those same sentences were joined together during re-arrangement, the result became smoother and more syntactically regular — ironically making it more AI-like.
      
      4. Non-text elements removed
      
      Tables, bullet points, or complex formatting can be ignored during AI assessment.
      If one version included them and the other did not (for example, if you merged recommendations into full paragraphs), the system would have more continuous text to scan, increasing the detected proportion.
      
      5. AI model sensitivity
      
      Turnitin itself admits that its detector is probabilistic and inconsistent between uploads.
      It does not “recognise” your previous file; it re-evaluates the text every time.
      So even identical wording can score differently if Turnitin’s parsing model interprets the sentence boundaries, line breaks, or style data differently on a new submission.
      
      In short
      
      The change in AI percentage has little to do with your actual writing.
      It is a product of:
      
      different paragraph order and formatting,
      
      Turnitin’s internal Word-to-PDF conversion,
      
      the amount of text classed as “qualifying” prose,
      
      and the algorithm’s probabilistic nature.
      
      If you want stable results, always:
      
      Use the same Word template and spacing,
      
      Keep consistent paragraph structure,
      
      Avoid merging or reordering sections before re-submission,
      
      Export as the same file type and upload only once.
      
      
      Did you know about this?

  1) Good
          a) Top notch (colloquial) „The hotel was nothing special, but the breakfast was top notch.“
          b) Outstanding (formal)
      2) Bad
          a) Lousy (colloquial) „The plumber did a lousy job. Water is leaking everywhere!“
          b) Appalling (formal, very bad)
      3) Great
          a) Awesome (colloquial) „The concert was awesome!“
          b) Tremendous (formal)
      4) Old
          a) Long in the tooth (colloquial; used for people) „I’m far too long in the tooth to listen to reggaeton.“
          b) Antiquated (formal) „For a young man, he has surprisingly antiquated views.“
      5) Young
          a) Childlike “She has an attractive childlike personality.”
          b) Childish “Stop being so childish and help your father!”
      6) Small/little
          a) Miniscule “For 16 years, we lived in a miniscule flat in the centre of the city.”
          b) Knee-high to a grasshopper “The last time I saw you, you were knee-high to a grasshopper!”
      7) Big/large
          a) gargantuan, colossal, enormous
          b) Humongous “If I were rich, I’d buy a humongous house in the country.”
      8) High
          a) Lofty “The lofty trees swayed in the wind.”, ”He had lofty goals of becoming CEO.”
      9) Different
          a) Chalk and cheese “My sister and I are chalk and cheese.”
          b) Disparate “We often clash because our political views are so disperate.”
      10) Same
          a) Peas in a pod “The brother were like peas in a pod.”
          b) Tantamount “Calling a Scot an Englishman is tantamount to a declaration of war.”

**@kolya_gtr** (👍4 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4wpjb5rvFZA&lc=UgwhqGMMzb6SCiMKSPN4AaABAg
  Phrasal verbs are easy to understand. Everything you need is to know meanings of the prepositions what placed after main verbs. For example, the very phrasal verb "keep up" - keep is to hold sth or continue to do sth and preposition "up" is as teacher said is to increase/improve sth or it's some movement or direction - I climb up the mountain or I walk down the stairs. In this case the preposition UP points to direction of movement. Now let's return to the word keep up - Keep it up means Continue improving it. As you can see, I simply put together 2 meanings and got the new word. That way you can learn a lot of different phrasal verbs. If you know meanings of the preposition what's used in your phrasal verb, you'll be able to learn a lot of phrasal verbs

  You are correct, but not by intuition.  'to stay up' can only be used as an active verb, meaning the subject does the action of 'not going to bed',  'to be kept up' is used in the passive here, meaning sb else does the action, which affects the subject.  Used in the active form, it means that you do sthg to stop sb from going to bed.  It's grammar, not just 'what sounds right'

**@deliapauline123** (👍28 · 2014-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7ZWXtyavnMw&lc=UghGygpzAZqLy3gCoAEC
  I agree that the emphasis with the present perfect simple is on the result rather than the action but is far more than a reference to quantity or numbers. For example, 'You've had your hair cut!' emphasises the result (a new look!) or I've lost my keys! (I can't get into my house) but these have nothing to do with numbers!
  It's important not to let a rule of thumb become an overgeneralisaiton or students will apply it indescriminately and this will confuse them more than anything else.
  Other examples of present perfect sentences that emphasise result but have nothing to do with numbers: 'I've let the dog out. ' 'I've had enough!' 
  Anyway, I like your videos and think they are clear and captivating

  Present perfect simple = The emphasis is on a time span we can resume with... (____your life up to now). EX I've never lived in Italy, I've always enjoyed cinema, Have you ever tried bunjee jumping?
  
  ALSO, we can use this tense with FOR and SINCE to talk about situations that began in the past and continue in the present.
  
  EX. I've lived here for ten years, I haven't seen her since last summer... etc.

  In high school, I was told by one or two teachers to NOT ask a question. However, I think in college things like that are a little less strict...
    ↳ **@shaneduckworth7288** (👍8 · 2015-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nWqMQ26Gqi4&lc=UghD9KXJ4KqNnXgCoAEC.7-H0Z7-J45c7-sL5crYjdM
      I think you're a bit confused about the question thing. What teachers mean when they say that is that your thesis should not BE a question. Your thesis should be the answer to the question and your essay will be about exploring and proving that answer. For instance, if you're asked to write a character analysis from the Harry Potter series, you start by asking questions: "Why did J. K. Rowling make up a character like...Nevel or Dobie or Snape?" "What role does that character play--physically, emotionally, philosophically?" For instance, if I picked Snape I could ask questions about who he really is (as opposed to how he showed himself throughout the books) and what lessons Rowling was maybe trying to teach us through this character. I might even be able to draw from real live people who chose to hide their true selves for the greater good (watch Valkyrie w/ Tom Cruise). My thesis would grow out from my answers to these questions. The real first step of an essay is to ask questions then RESEARCH for the answer. It's not to come up with your thesis and then "prove" it. This leads to looking for information that supports your thesis rather than allowing your thesis to develop from your understanding of a topic. Hope that clears things up for you.

**@XXXXcloudangellXXXX** (👍4 · 2016-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nWqMQ26Gqi4&lc=Ugg20CEALphG_ngCoAEC
  If essay is about internet: good or bad? [Easiest example]
  1st para:
  Intro
  Thesis statement
  Rhetorical question
  1 Advantage and 1 Disadvantage. 
  At least 5 sentences
  
  2nd para: 
  This paragraph can be an advantage or disadvantage. Take all the points in mind and connect them by linking words, very important. 
  
  3rd para:
  If it's a disadvantage, first line must be "On the contrary", then start with points followed by linking words. 
  
  4th para:
  The first line must be telling about the author's opinion. Conclude the whole essay by summarizing the whole thing in a sentence or two. 
  
  Well, this is what I learned at school, care to share yours?

**@Anna-mc3ll** (👍15 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gFXE9n7hrOI&lc=Ugy6Fb17er13uCj8_ul4AaABAg
  Descriptive writing:
  
  to plead - to make an urgent emotional statement or request for something
  
  to beg - to make a very strong and urgent request
  
  to entreat - to try very hard to persuade someone to do something
  
  to implore - to ask someone to do or not do something in a very sincere, emotional, and determined way
  
  to beseech - to ask for something in a way that shows you need it very much
  
  to cajole - to persuade someone to do something they might not want to do, by pleasant talk and promises
  
  to insist - to say firmly or demand forcefully, especially when others disagree or oppose what you say
  
  to demand - to ask for something forcefully, in a way that shows that you do not expect to be refused
  
  to gush - to express a positive feeling, especially praise, sometimes in such a strong way that it does not sound sincere
  
  to cheer - to give a loud shout of approval or encouragement
  
  to tout - to advertise, talk about, or praise something or someone repeatedly, especially as a way of encouraging people to like, accept, or buy something
  
  to laugh - to smile while making sounds with your voice that show you think something is funny or you are happy
  
  to chortle - to laugh, showing pleasure and satisfaction
  
  to giggle - to laugh repeatedly in a quiet but uncontrolled way, often at something silly or rude or when you are nervous
  
  to proclaim - to announce something publicly or officially, especially something positive
  
  to announce - to make something known or tell people about something officially
  
  to declare - to announce something clearly, firmly, publicly, or officially 
  
  to pout - to show annoyance, especially by pressing the lips together or pushing out the lower lip
  
  to complain - to say that something is wrong or not satisfactory
  
  to sob - to cry noisily, taking in deep breaths
  
  to cry - to produce tears as the result of a strong emotion, such as unhappiness or pain
  
  to lament - to express sadness and feeling sorry about something
  
  to sneer - to talk about someone or something in an unkind way that shows no respect
  
  to whine - to make a long, high, sad sound
  
  to bemoan - to complain or express sadness about something
  
  to shout - to speak with a very loud voice, often as loud as possible, usually when you want to make yourself heard in noisy situations
  
  to exclaim - to say or shout something suddenly because of surprise, fear, pleasure, etc.
  
  to bellow - to shout in a loud voice
  
  to murmur - to speak or say something very quietly
  
  to mutter - to speak quietly and in a low voice that is not easy to hear
  
  to mumble - to speak quietly and in a way that is not clear, so that the words are difficult to understand
  
  to whisper - to speak very quietly, so that only the person close to you can hear you

**@Mrradio01-15** (👍0 · 2026-07-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gFXE9n7hrOI&lc=UgzSZQS231yiInKZGtZ4AaABAg
  Very informative video! I haven’t written anything very much until a few years ago (2022) since high school and I am now 31. I enjoyed writing a lot in school thanks to a couple of very good teachers in elementary school and I thought I was ok at it. This video has given me much better skills! Now bear with me when I say this very crazy thing: Use a typewriter for your first drafts. I kid you not when I say that I find it very helpful for concentration and getting those initial thoughts onto paper. No distractions from the computer: It’s just you and the machine. No annoying notifications from emails, social media  or spell check  or other things like that I find very distracting. It will bug me until I go and make the corrections Microsoft Word  tells me to. Meanwhile, I have lost my train of thought of the initial purpose I was writing that sentence for. Trust me when I say that  first draft is going to be VERY ugly (grammar and spelling wise) if you’re not used to being without a computer like I was when you proofread it. HOWEVER, the thoughts will be completely yours. Typewriters are after all completely dependent  on you. It only puts onto paper what you tell it to. It makes you think about what you are writing, unless you like using white out or starting over 😂. The return is it will not judge your writing and it aids in the creative process. It’s all about getting those thoughts onto paper. I then take what I have done on the typewriter, proofread it as many times as I see fit, make corrections based on what I see and then fine tune it on the computer. I am still living in the 21st century too. As far as what typewriter to get, that is a different rabbit hole entirely but there are great people on YouTube who will help you out with that. I went from not knowing much about typewriters and a little curiosity to getting it and typing every word that I know like Ron Swanson from Parks and Recreation at my grandma’s house where I got my typewriter. Now I have my own method of writing that is fun and apparently there are communities of other people who think like I do! Happy writing and enjoy yourselves!

      The past perfect refers to a time earlier than before now. It is used to make it clear that one event happened before another in the past. It does not matter which event is mentioned first - the tense makes it clear which one happened first.  
      
      
      Had met: She had met him before the party. Had left: The plane had left by the time I got to the airport. Had written: I had written the email before he apologized.

    ↳ **@katiefoley7046** (👍0 · 2015-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=loE2_ztqQ64&lc=UgjT9EECkw4ocXgCoAEC.7-H0Z7-Opwv78KgVJLEGCf
      This is very difficult to explain but yes it is correct. You are talking about when to use the verbs 'say', 'tell', 'talk' and 'speak'. 
      
       SAY is used with direct and indirect speech for instance: She said that it was my last chance.
      Say is most often used without a personal object. for instance: He said, ‘Good morning.’
      If we want to put a personal object after say, we use 'to' of instance 'When I say to you that I am honest, I am honest".
      
      TELL is used with direct and indirect speech
      after  the word tell, we usually say who is told, i.e., tell someone something for instance: She told me that she would be late and She told me that it was my last chance (not He told them, ‘Good morning.’)
      Tell is only used to mean ‘instruct’ or ‘inform’ for instance: 
      Tell is used to tell someone to do something for instance :Tom’s mother told him to clean his room.
      Tell is not used before objects like a word, a name, a sentence, a phrase 
      We do not usually use it after tell to refer to a fact for instance: I’ll tell you tomorrow.’ (not I’ll tell you it tomorrow.) 
      
      TALK
      There is not very much difference between speak and talk.
      Talk is the more usual word to refer to conversational exchanges and informal communication, for instance: When she walked into the room everybody stopped talking.
      
      SPEAK
      Speak is often used for one-way communication and for exchanges in more serious or formal situations for instance: I’ll have to speak to that boy -- he’s getting very lazy.
      Speak is the usual word to refer to knowledge and use of languages for instance: After she had finished reading the letter, nobody spoke.
      She speaks three languages fluently.

  Dear James, I completely disagree with you. 
  Eg. He made her cry. 
  There are two clauses in the above sentence: Finite clause (He made) and non-finite clause (her cry). You should read more about modern linguistics.
    ↳ **@valentinaespinosa7894** (👍0 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=loE2_ztqQ64&lc=UgiRsrzDIGmw2HgCoAEC.8NQ--W8DqN58WDLEaKlP-Z
      Bùi Ngọc Linh No, the clause doesn't stop at make because it wouldn't make sense. Make is a monotransitive verb in that example so it needs both the indirect object and direct object there to be an independent clause.
    ↳ **@syubidubidu3193** (👍0 · 2018-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=loE2_ztqQ64&lc=UgiRsrzDIGmw2HgCoAEC.8NQ--W8DqN58aiTio_3Cm_
      Pronoun cannot stand by its own. Hence it cannot make it into a new clause, because 'her' here functions as the object not a subject.

  I have been used to waking up at 7 am for 1 year etc. With the expression, 'I used to...' you always use an infinitive after it, i.e. I used to wake up at 6 am; I didn't use to wake up at 6 am (conjugates like a normal verb). You always use, 'I used to in the simple past or past perfect simple tenses, i.e. I used to go swimming (verb 'to go' is in the infinitive, while swimming is a gerund); I had used to go swimming before I started running.

  In a sentence, yes: 'I had been used to using running as a means to improving breathing capacity, but I now I am starting to become used to going swimming as a means to improving it'; In a parallel clause (or list), no: I used to run, swim and walk... (not I used to run, swim and walking...) Basically, with the expression, 'I am used to...' you always use a gerund after it (the tense doesn't matter), i.e I am used to waking up at 6 am; I was used to waking up at 7 am;

    ↳ **@KpopKnitter** (👍2 · 2015-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ulezklvGaQk&lc=UgiR5p3Adh3Xa3gCoAEC.7-H0Z7-5A_j70e-PpZX7MZ
      As James explained "used to" is something that you did in the past. "Get used to" means that you could do something regularly. For example, if I say "I could get used to making a lot of money", it means something like "I am starting to make more money and it is something that I would like to do/ or have happen regularly". Basically, "get used to" means that something is becoming a normal process or thing in your life. Let's look at another example. If I said "I got used to waking up early for school". This sentence means something like "I did not like waking up early before, but now that I have to, it has become a normal thing in my life". I hope this helps!

**@mattdobz** (👍15 · 2015-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUrTT9I9wXA&lc=UgiUFP_VYTgLtHgCoAEC
  Proper nouns are awkward. If you have to use an apostrophe like the plural sense because a singular word ends in 's', you pronounce the word as if it doesn't have an apostrophe (e.g. James' pen would be said as "James pen", not "James-is pen"). If you need to indicate that you are saying James' (/d͡ʒeɪmz/) and not James (/ˈd͡ʒeɪms/), you subtly prolong and constrict the 's' to create a buzz similar to a 'z'. Adding an -is suffix to the pronunciation makes it more difficult to say (try saying "Jesus-is disciples" multiple times very quickly). This rule does apply to some regular nouns.
  
  When using "it's", you are using the shortened form of "it is" (e.g. it's a lovely day). To indicate possession to "it", the apostrophe is removed (e.g. a lion and its cubs).
    ↳ **@M_JackOfAllTrades** (👍1 · 2023-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUrTT9I9wXA&lc=UgiUFP_VYTgLtHgCoAEC.82h36fzIAIw9gaFZLepoHL

  If you're an English professor, you must be familiar with the MLA style guide, the standard for academic writing in English. Please refer to the MLA handbook, rule 2.2.7e:
  
  "To form the possessive of any singular proper noun, add an apostrophe and an s."
  
  And the examples it gives are:
  
  Venus's beauty
  Dickens's reputation
  Descartes's philosophy
  
  Dozens of university websites confirm that this is the rule.
  
  Don't feel bad -- you learn something new every day.

  quote from grammar book:
  
  If I were / if I was
  After if and wish, you can use were instead of was (if I were / I wish it were etc.).
  If I was / I wish it was are also possible. So you can say:
  
  -  If I were you, I wouldn't buy that coat.      or If I was you, ...
  -  I'd go for a walk if it weren't so cold.         or ... if it wasn't so cold.
  -  I wish she were here.                                    or I wish she was here.
  
  end of quote. 
  
  So "I was" also possible but not common I think.

  Phrasal verb is simply a verb with a preposition that has a greater meaning
  
  E.g. Cheer means to root for smo, to motivate or support smo, whereas Cheer up, implies making smo happy when they're sad
  
  The word UP has a couple of meanings in combination with some verbs: 
  1. Increase — add up, speak up, cheer up, jack up or make up or bring up
  2. Move — catch up, speed up, go up, walk up
  3. Complete — wrap up, finish up, end up

  I'd like to finish this up later.
  
  PHARASAL VERB = 2 OR 3 WORDS word
  Verb + preposition (+preposition)
  
  Up + Verb = #1. Increase #2. Movement #3. Complete(ment)
  
  Don't bring up this topic as it's too sensitive for us
  
  COMPLETE:
  You've got to put gas into the tank so to fill up the fuel
  I will finish up reading my homework a bit later
  MOVE: 
  We should catch up to reach them
  If you run up to him during a race it might be possible but unlikely
  INCREASE: 
  Speak up I want to listen to you lucidly 
  Could you turn up the volume of TV set I don't here anything
  Cheer up you shouldn't be sad! You're  alive you have a home with healthy parents who care about you.
  Why don't you grow up If you're acting like a little kid
  
  THE KEY TO GET THE "UP" preposition in PHRASAL VERBS
  INCREASE MOVE AND COMPLETE
  
  There 3 uses of up in PHRASAL VERB combination: to increase, to move, to complete
  
  I want to add up some strength for my body
  Be careful you must not even walk up to this animal! Otherwise he will devour you completely!! Beware

  Your explanation is not quite correct. You use "must" when it is your decision (based on facts, belief, or something else - doesn't matter), i.e., it is important for you, but you have a choice not to do it.  You use "have to" when circumstances make you do something-you don't have a choice not to do it.

  Hold — keep it in same place or maintain the position
  
  Hold on — wait for a moment/minute also means keeping your arms tightly around smth so you wouldn't fall down

  Hold your peace — shut up, when smo is about to be dead
  Hold your tongue — shut up
  Hold up — waiting, smth is making one wait
  Hold my own — keep up with being as good as anyone else; TO DO WELL in a difficult situation;e.g. I was holding my own even when it was hard the last summer
  Hold my ground — not gonna change your position

**@Cloudbusting2024** (👍5 · 2011-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8CiA9BCRPBk&lc=Ugxs2IaZZlKcR-9KKzB4AaABAg
  Hi James, great video but...
  
  'The' is NOT only for singular objects. 
  
  Examples:
  The dog. The dogs.  The pen. The pens. The man. The men.  Singular and plural.
  
  a & an are for singular objects.
  
  Also...
  a is followed by a consonant SOUND.    an is followed by a vowel SOUND.
  
  an hour     The h is a consonant but not a consonant sound. Hour starts with a vowel SOUND....the same as our. (Crazy English!)
  
  Thanks for THE video. It was A pleasure. THE pleasure was all mine.  :)

  For comprehension you have to understand the context (meaning)
  IN OTHER WORDS, even if you don't understand some words you'll still be able to get the gist 
  
  #1 — Read everything 
  
  #2 — Read again with dictionary and summarize each PARAGRAPH 
  
  #3 — Read once more, this time you understand the whole article and summarize everything you've read
  
  By reading over and over you learn idioms and words, you comprehend the meaning deeper
  
  #4 — Read on daily basis anything in English as a habit

  Comprehesion is a skill of understanding 
  – One may read a book, but not truly understand the meaning
  
  Context — when you don't understand all the words and but the meaning 
  
  Get the book you need and then
  #1. FOCUS ON CONTEXT, Read quickly and underline the words you don't know (don't use the dictionary) FOCUS on the context, get the gist
  #2. READ AGAIN. Use Your Dictionary and Summarize Each Paragraph
  #3. READ IT AGAIN. Summarize Everything We've Read (you'll deeply learn the skill to cut down your reading time!!)
  
  Reading over and over again for a month you'll get YOU the real result
